claim: An earthquake is shaking of the earth caused by sudden release of energy along a fault; the release point underground is the focus (hypocentre) and the surface point directly above it is the epicentre, which feels the waves first
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
note: USGS uses the same two terms (focus or hypocenter; epicenter).

claim: Damage is usually greatest closest to the epicentre and the strength decreases with distance; USGS adds that the highest observed intensity generally occurs near the epicentre
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch3 Our Changing Earth (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
page_or_section: p.13 (Our Changing Earth > Earthquake case study opening; Fig 3.3)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
note: Class 7 wording: strength decreases away from the centre. 'Usually': a soft-soil site far away can shake more (our inference, not sourced).

claim: Why the ground breaks: rocks along a fault are pressed together and locked by friction; stress builds until the blocks slide past each other abruptly and release energy as waves
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
note: USGS: energy is stored in the rocks and released suddenly by shearing along faults. Classic 'stick-slip' picture; the word elastic rebound is not used by either source.

claim: Earthquake waves are of two families: body waves (P and S) that travel through the earth, and surface waves made when body waves reach the surface; P arrives first, S next, surface waves last and are the most destructive
value: P, S, surface; arrival order P-S-L
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Interior of the Earth'
note: USGS interior text confirms P = compressional and S = shear waves; it does not give arrival order or damage ranking, so those two points are NCERT-only.

claim: P waves are like sound waves and pass through solids, liquids and gases; S waves pass only through solids. Because S waves stop at the outer core, scientists infer that it is liquid
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
page_or_section: p.20 (P and S waves); also p.23 (The Core)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Interior of the Earth'
note: USGS: outer core presumed liquid because it does not transmit S waves. This is the evidence link to the Interior-of-the-Earth episode (GEO-01).

claim: Shadow zones: seismographs within 105 degrees of the epicentre record both P and S waves; between 105 and 145 degrees neither wave type arrives; beyond 105 degrees no S waves arrive, so the S shadow covers a little over 40 per cent of the earth
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Single source (NCERT). USGS interior text gives no angles. NCERT wording in one sentence is loose: it says seismographs beyond 145 degrees record P but not S, while the S shadow is described as everything beyond 105 degrees. Teach: P shadow band 105-145; S shadow all beyond 105.

claim: Class 7 names three earthquake wave types: P (longitudinal), S (transverse) and L (surface) waves
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch3 Our Changing Earth (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Class XI names the same three but calls the third 'surface waves'. Same idea, two labels; teach both.

claim: NCERT lists five kinds of earthquake by cause: tectonic (most common), volcanic, collapse (mine roofs), explosion and reservoir-induced
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Class XI India PE (p.55) agrees tectonic ones are the most devastating and widest in reach, while volcanic, rockfall, landslide, subsidence and reservoir quakes have limited area. Reservoir-induced is the Koyna link, but NCERT does not say so.

claim: NCERT says magnitude is measured on the Richter scale (energy released, numbers 0 to 10) and intensity on the Mercalli scale (visible damage, 1 to 12). USGS says the Richter scale has no upper limit, that the Modified Mercalli scale has 12 levels in Roman numerals, and that it is based on observed effects
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
note: NCERT's '0-10' is a teaching simplification, not a limit. Intensity is a place-by-place ranking of effects; magnitude is one instrument-based number per earthquake.

claim: Magnitude is related to the seismic energy released at the focus and is one instrumentally determined number; intensity is based on observed effects of shaking on people, buildings and land and varies from place to place
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
second_source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
note: This is the exact UPSC 2019 Geography Q4a pair: methods of measuring intensity and magnitude.

claim: Each whole step of magnitude is a tenfold rise in recorded ground-motion amplitude and about 31 to 32 times more energy released
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
second_source: USGS Publications Warehouse record: Johnston 1990, 'An earthquake strength scale for the media and the public' (abstract)
note: USGS 1989 text says about 31; USGS Johnston 1990 abstract says 32. Both mean 10 to the power 1.5. Our arithmetic: a magnitude 9.1 releases about 32 times the energy of an 8.1 and about 1,000 times a 7.1 (1.5 x 2 steps on the power).

claim: The USGS catalog now records big earthquakes as moment magnitude: the 26 Dec 2004 Sumatra earthquake is M 9.1 (type mw) and the 26 Jan 2001 Bhuj earthquake is M 7.7 (type mwc). A 1990 USGS publication already says the Richter scale was no longer used
source: USGS ComCat earthquake catalog, FDSN event web service (official API)
second_source: USGS Publications Warehouse record: Johnston 1990, 'An earthquake strength scale for the media and the public' (abstract)
note: The USGS explainer pages on 'magnitude types' sit behind a bot-check (usgs.gov returned HTTP 202 with no content); they were NOT read. This claim stands on the catalog data and the 1990 abstract only. Do not quote the 'saturation' explanation from memory.

claim: USGS current-page statements on moment magnitude, Richter saturation and the energy formula
note: usgs.gov pages return an empty bot-check page to plain fetch and to the reading tool; not bypassed. Use G3-A12 (catalog) and G3-A11 instead.

claim: India's National Seismological Network (170 observatories, April 2026) detects and locates earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above anywhere in India, and NCS processes the data in near real time to make earthquake parameters and ShakeMaps (intensity maps)
source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Parliament Question: Seismograph Network (Lok Sabha, 1 Apr 2026)
page_or_section: reply text, paras on NSN (Lok Sabha, 1 Apr 2026, by Dr Jitendra Singh)
second_source: National Center for Seismology (MoES), official website home page
note: seismo.gov.in home says 'more than 170 stations'. Older replies gave 115, 152 or 166: network counts change, show with the date. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Reply read correctly (Dr Jitendra Singh, MoS (IC) Earth Sciences, Lok Sabha, 1 Apr 2026; 170 observatories; M3.0+). Its station table lists only the 14 stations in Himachal Pradesh and Karnataka. Older counts in saved files: 115 (PIB 1740656, 30 Jul 2021) and 166 (PIB 2085953, 19 Dec 2024); no saved file gives 152, so drop '152'.

claim: In India, shaking strength in the building-code context is described on the MSK intensity scale: NDMA says about 59 per cent of the land area is prone to shaking of MSK intensity VII and above
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: Single source. The MSK-64 scale definition and BIS's own statement of which scale the code uses were not read: see G3-A16.

claim: Definition of the MSK (Medvedev-Sponheuer-Karnik) intensity scale and BIS's statement of the intensity scale used in IS 1893
note: Only the NDMA mention in G3-A15 was found. BIS standard text is paywalled/not opened. If the script needs MSK, say only 'a 12-level intensity scale like Mercalli' and name MSK as used by NDMA.

claim: Plate boundaries: where continents collide they make fold mountains such as the Himalaya; where an oceanic plate meets a continental plate the oceanic one sinks, giving volcanoes and earthquakes; at divergent boundaries magma makes new crust; transform boundaries slide past and mainly cause earthquakes, as along the San Andreas fault
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 1, Ch2 Shaping of the Earth's Surface (First ed. June 2026)
second_source: USGS This Dynamic Earth, Plate tectonics and people
note: USGS: most earthquakes and volcanoes occur in belts at plate boundaries, not at random.

claim: Most earthquakes happen at plate boundaries: USGS (1989 text) says about 90 per cent of the world's earthquakes occur in belts at the boundaries of the major crustal plates, and its 'Earthquakes' publication says fewer than 10 per cent occur within plate interiors
source: USGS General Interest Publication 'The Severity of an Earthquake' (1989 text)
page_or_section: caption of the epicentre map, 'The Severity of an Earthquake'
second_source: USGS General Interest Publication 'Earthquakes', Where Earthquakes Occur
note: Both are old USGS publications; the numbers are USGS's own wording and not a 2026 recount. Row 2020-GS1-4-05 in the audited PYQ ledger reads the second one.

claim: Himalayan earthquakes: NCERT says the Indian plate moves about one centimetre a year north and north-east and is obstructed by the Eurasian plate; the plates lock, stress builds, and the sudden release causes earthquakes along the Himalayan arc
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: USGS This Dynamic Earth, Plate tectonics and people
note: USGS This Dynamic Earth confirms the India-Eurasia collision crumpled the crust into the Himalaya. The '1 cm/yr' figure is NCERT-only; no allowed source for the plate speed was read this run, so show it as 'NCERT says about a centimetre a year' and do not add another figure.

claim: NDMA lists four great Himalayan earthquakes in about 50 years: Shillong 1897 (M 8.7), Kangra 1905 (M 8.0), Bihar-Nepal 1934 (M 8.3) and Assam-Tibet 1950 (M 8.6), and says the whole Himalayan region is vulnerable to magnitude 8 or more
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: Single source. Magnitudes are NDMA's quoted values (it writes 'Richter Scale'; modern catalogues re-estimate old events). Say 'NDMA lists'.

claim: The Peninsula is not earthquake-proof: the 1967 Koyna and 1993 Latur earthquakes broke the belief that regions away from plate boundaries are safe, and led to revisions of the seismic zoning map. NCERT notes Gujarat (1819, 1956, 2001) and Maharashtra (1967, 1993) had severe quakes and mentions a possible fault line along the Bhima near Latur
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT p.56 also says the Deccan plateau is largely safe (p.57): both can be true; 'safest' is relative, not 'safe'.

claim: India's major earthquakes in the 1990s-2000s named by NDMA: Uttarkashi 1991, Latur 1993, Jabalpur 1997, Chamoli 1999, Bhuj 26 Jan 2001 and Jammu and Kashmir 8 Oct 2005; NDMA counts 6 major earthquakes from 1990 to 2006 with over 23,000 deaths, and says most casualties came from collapse of buildings
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: This is the list the UPSC 2021 GS3 Q8 asks for (vulnerability and salient features of recent major quakes). Deaths for each single quake were not read here except Bhuj (G3-A52). The post-2007 Indian quakes (Sikkim 2011, Nepal 2015 effects in India, Manipur 2016) were NOT read. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Per-quake deaths for Bhuj are in G3-A61, not G3-A52 (that id is the ITEWC RTSP row).

claim: NCERT describes five earthquake damage-risk zones (very high to very low) from an analysis of more than 1,200 earthquakes; but BIS's zoning map used by the building code has four zones (II to V): NDMA's table of the IS 1893 (2002) map has only zones II, III, IV and V
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
page_or_section: pp.56-57 (Due to an Earthquake); Fig 6.2 p.58
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: NDMA07 Table 2, p.10. The merge of the old Zone I into II happened in the 2002 edition (our reading of the table; the standard itself was not opened). Teach the BIS four-zone map; mention NCERT's 'five' as the older textbook count. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Support for 'four zones' is indirect: NDMA 2007 Table 2 (IS 1893:2002 map) and MoES Lok Sabha reply 12 Mar 2021 (PIB 1704836: 'four seismic zones') and the 1 Apr 2026 reply's table labelled 'as per IS 1893 (Part-1):2016' (zones II-V seen, but only for 14 stations in two states). The BIS standard itself was not opened. NCERT kegy106 p.56 five zones and 1,200+ earthquakes confirmed. Both sides read correctly; CONFLICT kept.

claim: The seismic zoning map of India published by BIS in IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 'remains the current standard'; the revised zonation was withdrawn in March 2026 (Lok Sabha reply, 1 April 2026)
source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Parliament Question: Seismograph Network (Lok Sabha, 1 Apr 2026)
page_or_section: reply text, last paragraph before the monitoring paragraph
note: Living fact; check again before release. Single government source (Minister's reply via PIB). BIS's own gazette/notice of the withdrawal was not found (G3-A25). The reply's station table lists zones II, III, IV and V only (5, 2, 3 and 4 stations). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Reply read correctly: the sentence says the 2016 map 'remains the current standard' and the 'revised zonation has been withdrawn in March 2026'; answered by Dr Jitendra Singh, MoS (IC) Earth Sciences and S&T, in Lok Sabha on 1 Apr 2026 (PIB 11:52 on the same day). It does not say who withdrew it or what the revised map was. Context found in audit: MoES reply PIB 2205330 (17 Dec 2025, saved) described the 'updated seismic zonation map' with Himalayan arc in Zone VI, so the withdrawn revision is the one with Zone VI. Still one government source for the withdrawal; no BIS notice.

claim: BIS / Gazette of India notice of the 2025 revision (IS 1893 (Part 1):2025, with a new highest-risk Zone VI for the Himalayan arc) and of its withdrawal in March 2026
note: Web search shows many coaching sites describing a Zone VI; ignore them. The only primary text read is the Lok Sabha reply (G3-A24) that says the revised zonation was withdrawn. A BIS CED 39 listing may still show the 2025 edition for sale (seen in a search snippet only). Do NOT teach Zone VI as law. If mentioned at all: 'a revised map with a sixth zone was brought out in 2025 and withdrawn in March 2026' needs a BIS or Gazette source first. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Partial primary source found in audit: MoES reply on PIB (PRID 2205330, 17 Dec 2025, sources/mha/pib_2205330) says the 'updated seismic zonation map' puts the entire Himalayan arc in Zone VI and a small part of Ladakh in Zone V. It names no standard number or year. BIS/Gazette notice and the withdrawal notice still not found. Do not teach Zone VI as law; if mentioned: 'an updated map with Zone VI was cited by MoES in Dec 2025; MoES said in Apr 2026 it was withdrawn'.

claim: Area shares by zone: NDMA (IS 1893, 2002 map): zone II 41.4%, III 30.4%, IV 17.3%, V 10.9%, so 58.6% in zones III-V. MoES (Lok Sabha, 2021, zoning map then in use): about 59% of land is prone to earthquakes; about 11% in zone V, 18% in IV, 30% in III, rest in II
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
second_source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Earthquake Early Warning System (15 Mar 2021)
note: Both agree. The 2016-map shares themselves were not read in a BIS document; the 2021 MoES reply is the newest statement of shares found. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] The 2021 MoES reply was a written Lok Sabha reply of 12 Mar 2021 by Dr Harsh Vardhan; PIB posted it 15 Mar 2021 (as_of is the PIB date). NDMA Table 2 on p.10 confirmed (41.40, 30.40, 17.30, 10.90; bracket 58.6%).

claim: How zones are made: NDMA says the map marks areas of low, moderate and high hazard 'based on past trends' (historical earthquakes), and calls for a map based on return-period design accelerations, revised in phases starting with the Himalaya, North-East and west. NCERT says the zones came from analysing 1,200+ earthquakes by the National Geophysical Laboratory, Geological Survey of India, Department of Meteorology and NIDM (NCERT's names)
value: past-quake based; probabilistic revision called for
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Answers 'how are seismic zones demarcated' (UPSC 2019 Geography Q4a, 2020 Geography Q7a). The method of IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 itself was not opened. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NCERT kegy106 p.56 names National Geophysical Laboratory, GSI, Department of Meteorology and NIDM; 'NGRI' and 'IMD' were our expansions.

claim: NCERT lists the parts of India in the very high risk zone (North-East states, north of Darbhanga and Araria on the Indo-Nepal border in Bihar, Uttarakhand, western Himachal around Dharamshala, Kashmir Valley, Kuchchh) and high risk zone (rest of J&K, Ladakh, Himachal, north Punjab, east Haryana, Delhi, west UP, north Bihar); the stable Deccan is called the safest
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Single source; based on the older 5-zone map. The 2016-map zone of each city/state was not mapped here. Do not show city zones unless read from the 2016 map or an official table (the 2021 PIB replies carry city lists in zone IV and V and could be read for that).

claim: The National Center for Seismology under the Ministry of Earth Sciences is the Government of India's nodal agency for monitoring earthquake activity; it runs the National Seismological Network and shares data with insurers, river-valley projects and other users
source: National Center for Seismology (MoES), official website home page
second_source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Parliament Question: Seismograph Network (Lok Sabha, 1 Apr 2026)
note: PIB reply: NCS is the nodal agency for installing, operating and maintaining the stations; funds under the PRITHVI scheme.

claim: Earthquakes cannot be predicted in time, place and magnitude anywhere in the world; India only has a pilot Earthquake Early Warning project (IIT Roorkee, Uttarakhand, 2017) that would give seconds to about a minute of notice. Class 7 NCERT also says earthquakes cannot be predicted and lists animal-behaviour folk signs as local practice
source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Early Warning for Tsunami and Earthquake (29 Mar 2017)
second_source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch3 Our Changing Earth (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
note: Dated (2017). Whether a national earthquake early warning system exists in 2026 was not read. NCERT p.14 treats animal signs as 'methods adopted locally'; no source here says they work, so use as a guess-first myth, not a fact. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] 2017 PIB read correctly. Newer: MoES reply PIB 2205330 (17 Dec 2025) says NCS is 'making steady and systematic progress toward' an operational EEW system (10 P-Alert instruments in Himachal), i.e. none national yet; PIB 1704836 (Mar 2021) said no proven system. Say 'pilot, not national'.

claim: Class 7 earthquake safety advice: shelter under a kitchen counter, table or desk or against an inside corner or wall; keep away from fireplaces, chimneys, and windows or mirrors that shatter; spread awareness
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch3 Our Changing Earth (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
note: Single source (NCERT). NDMA/NIDM household do's and don'ts pages were not read. For on-screen safety advice add an NDMA source first.

claim: 'Tsunami' is Japanese for 'harbour wave'; NOAA says tsunamis are not related to tides, so 'tidal wave' is the wrong name
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
note: NOAA FAQ 1.2-1.3.

claim: NCERT Class 7 calls a tsunami 'a huge tidal wave', which NOAA calls incorrect: the wave has nothing to do with tides
value: tsunami is not a tidal wave
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
note: Good 'spot the mistake' item. NCERT Class 11 p.59 also lists 'tidal waves' separately from 'tsunami' in the aquatic hazards table (Table 6.1). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Correction: NCERT Class 11 Table 6.1 (tidal waves listed beside tsunami) is on p.55 of kegy106, not p.59.

claim: A tsunami is caused by a large and sudden displacement of the ocean. Large earthquakes below or near the sea floor are the commonest cause; landslides, volcanic activity, weather and meteorite impacts can also do it. In NOAA's global historical database 88 per cent were caused by earthquakes or earthquake-triggered landslides
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: NDMA10 Exec. Summary p.xxii also lists volcanic eruptions, submarine landslides, nuclear explosions and meteorite impacts. NCERT Class 11 p.59 names earthquakes and volcanic eruptions only.

claim: Mechanism: most tsunami-making earthquakes are thrust (reverse) faults in subduction zones where plates move toward each other; the sea floor lifts or drops, and the water above moves with it. About 10 to 15 per cent of damaging tsunamis come from strike-slip quakes, probably via landslides or slopes
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: NDMA10: vertical tectonic displacement of the sea bottom along a zone of fracture. NCERT Class 7 p.34 describes the 2004 mechanism: Indian plate going under the Burma plate, sea floor displaced.

claim: Threshold conflict: NOAA says most tsunamis come from earthquakes above magnitude 7.0 that are shallower than 100 km and near subduction zones, and a dangerous distant tsunami generally needs more than 8.0; NDMA says most are caused by earthquakes above 6.5; NCERT Class 11 says quake effects are devastating above 5 and a tsunami needs an epicentre under the ocean and 'sufficiently high' magnitude
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: NDMA10 Exec. Summary pp.xxi-xxii (it writes 'Richter Scale'). NCERT Class 11 p.21. Same idea, different cut-offs for different purposes (warning trigger v typical cause). India's own warning chart uses 6.5 and depth under 100 km (G3-A46). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Each side read correctly (NOAA FAQ 2.2: >7.0, <100 km, near subduction zones; >8.0 for dangerous distant; NDMA Exec. Summary p.xxii: 'more than 6.5'; NCERT kegy203 p.21: >5 for devastating effects, tsunami needs sub-ocean epicentre and 'sufficiently high' magnitude). Fixes: the India warning chart (M>6.5, depth <100 km) is in G3-A56, not G3-A46. The note 'different purposes' is our inference: NOAA 7.0 and NDMA 6.5 are both 'most tsunamis' statements, so they truly differ; NDMA 6.5 is also its warning trigger.

claim: Speed depends on depth, not distance: in the deep ocean a tsunami moves as fast as a jet, over 500 mph (about 800 km/h); near land it slows to about 20 to 30 mph. Speed equals the square root of depth times gravity: about 475 mph in 15,000 ft of water
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT Class 11 p.59 has the speed backwards: it says speed is more in shallow water than in the deep ocean (the first sentences of the Tsunami section). NOAA: deeper water, faster wave. Class 7 p.35 is right (700-900 km/h falling to under 70 km/h near India). Good spot-the-mistake item. Also: NCERT Class 7 p.35: 700-900 km/h falling to under 70 km/h near India; NCERT Class 7 p.34 says more than 700 km/h. Metric conversion of NOAA's mph is ours (1 mph = 1.609 km/h).

claim: In the deep ocean a tsunami is barely noticeable: height rarely over about a metre (3 ft) with a wavelength of hundreds of miles (NOAA FAQ 3.3; NOAA NCEI says hundreds of kilometres), so ships at sea do not notice it; near land the wavelength shortens, the wave slows and grows in height
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT Class 11 p.59: ship is lifted a metre or two, each rise and fall takes several minutes; period stays the same while wavelength shortens (NCERT-only point). Analogy for screen: a slow, wide hill passing under a boat; it stops being true because a tsunami is a whole water column moving, not a surface ripple. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NOAA tsunami.gov FAQ 3.3 says 'hundreds of miles'; 'hundreds of kilometres' is NOAA NCEI/NGDC's wording (ngdc_intro). Rarely over three feet confirmed.

claim: A tsunami is a series of waves (a wave train), the first need not be the largest, and a large one can last days; most tsunamis are under about 10 ft (3 m) at the coast but can exceed 100 ft near the source, and a large one can flood more than a mile inland. NCERT Grade 9 gives run-up up to 30 m or more in extreme cases; NCERT Class 11 gives 15 m or more
value: series; run-up <3 m typical; >30 m extreme
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch1 Oceans and Life (First ed. Sept 2026)
note: NCERT Grade 9 Part 2 p.5 defines run-up as maximum vertical height above sea level reached on shore. NOAA NGDC defines runup as maximum height of water above a reference sea level. Same idea.

claim: NCERT Class 7 says the largest tsunami ever measured was 150 m high. NOAA's database records a 1958 landslide-generated wave in Lituya Bay, Alaska that stripped trees to about 525 m (and a tsunami of at least 50 m in the bay)
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NOAA NCEI/NGDC, Introduction to Global Historical Tsunami Data
note: The two are not the same measure (NCERT unnamed; NOAA splash height up the slope). Do not repeat NCERT's 150 m. If a record is needed, name the event and the measure.

claim: Natural warning signs: strong or long ground shaking, a sudden recession of the sea that exposes the sea floor (like a very low tide), bubbling or a colour change, are cues to go to high ground at once; NCERT Class 7 says that in 2004 many onlookers gathered at the beach to watch the sea withdraw and died
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
second_source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
note: NOAA FAQ 3.4: the sea may recede suddenly. NCERT Class 7 p.35 gives the onlooker story. NDMA says local knowledge of the receding shoreline should be documented and shared.

claim: Seismic waves travel about 100 times faster than tsunamis, so earthquake data reach a warning centre before the tsunami; centres judge from location, depth and magnitude whether to warn
source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: Basis of all warning chains. Also the reason that coasts very near the source (Andaman and Nicobar, Sumatra coast) may have under an hour or far less (G3-A46).

claim: Where: NCERT says tsunamis are frequent along the Pacific ring of fire; NOAA says the highest hazard is on coasts near subduction zones. NDMA names five potential source regions for tsunamis reaching India: the Andaman-Nicobar-Sumatra island arc, Indo-Burmese zone, a 'nascent boundary' in the central Indian Ocean, the Chagos archipelago, and the Makran subduction zone; for warning, two are treated as the known tsunamigenic zones: the Java-Sumatra-Andaman-Myanmar belt and the North Arabian Sea
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
second_source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
note: NCERT Class 11 p.59 lists the Pacific rim. Class 7 p.35 says tsunamis are rare in the Indian Ocean because seismic activity is lower than the Pacific; this is NCERT-only reasoning.

claim: Makran earthquake of 27 Nov 1945 (Ms 8.3): waves of 12 to 15 m at Ormara and 13 m at Pasni in present-day Pakistan; an estimated 11 m in the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) and about 2 m at Mumbai, where boats were torn from moorings
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
page_or_section: Annexure table of major tsunamis, row 9 (printed p.122)
note: Single source (NDMA's tsunami history table). A western-coast example that fits the 'why some coasts' title: the Arabian Sea has a source too. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NDMA's own text is inconsistent: Annexure row 9 gives Ms 8.3 (used here, plus 1.37 m at Karachi), while Section 1.2.1 gives Ms 8.2, maximum run-up 13 m in Pakistan and 4,000 deaths. Show 8.2-8.3 or name the page.

claim: 26 Dec 2004: the Sumatra-Andaman earthquake had moment magnitude 9.1 per USGS (epicentre about 3.3 N, 96.0 E, depth 30 km, near 00:58 UTC = about 6:28 IST in the catalog), NCERT Class 7 says 9.0 'on the Richter scale' and NDMA writes MW 9.3
source: USGS ComCat earthquake catalog, FDSN event web service (official API)
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: NCERT Class 7 p.34; NDMA10 annexure row 10 (printed p.122). Local clock conversion is ours. Use the USGS 9.1 and say sources differ (9.0 to 9.3); some later studies revise it but none was read.

claim: The 2004 earthquake occurred on the megathrust where the India plate goes under the Burma plate off northern Sumatra; NOAA calls it the tsunami that killed more people than any other in recorded history
source: NOAA NCEI/NGDC, Introduction to Global Historical Tsunami Data
second_source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
note: NCERT Class 7 p.34 says the Indian plate went under the Burma plate, the sea floor shifted 10 to 20 m and tilted, water first withdrew then rushed back; NCERT-only numbers.

claim: Total toll of 2004 differs by source: NOAA NCEI 227,899 killed or missing and 1,126,900 displaced; NDMA 238,000 casualties including 51,500 missing and over 1.5 million displaced in 14 countries; NCERT Grade 9 says around 2,30,000 lives; Grade 6 says more than two lakh; Class 11 India PE says more than 300,000
source: NOAA NCEI/NGDC, Introduction to Global Historical Tsunami Data
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: NDMA10 §1.3.1 p.2. NCERT: Grade 9 Pt 2 p.12; Grade 6 Ch2 p.34; Class 11 India PE p.59 ('more than 300,000'). Class 11's figure is the outlier. Counts of 'missing' differ. Teach 'about 2.3 lakh across 14 countries'.

claim: India's toll in 2004: NDMA gives 10,749 dead and 5,640 missing in the tsunami-affected areas. NCERT Class 7 (old) says more than 10,000; new NCERT Grade 7 Part 2 says some 15,000; NCERT lists the worst hit as Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Puducherry and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
second_source: NCERT Grade 7 Exploring Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch2 India and Her Neighbours (Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT sources: Class 7 old p.35, Grade 7 Pt 2 p.56, Grade 9 Pt 2 p.12. 10,749 + 5,640 = 16,389 (our sum). NCERT '15,000' roughly lumps the two. Official toll in later MHA years not re-read. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NCERT lists differ: old Class 7 p.35 names Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry, A&N (and 'more than 10,000'); Grade 7 Part 2 says 'some 15,000' in India, 'especially Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands'. Do not merge the lists.

claim: NCERT Class 7 p.34-35 says Indira Point, India's southernmost point, was completely submerged by the 2004 tsunami
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
note: No allowed official source on Indira Point's state was read. Do not repeat 'completely submerged' on screen without a source (the lighthouse and the point's land level change are not covered by what we read).

claim: On Simeulue island (Indonesia) the island was 'largely spared' in 2004 and, NCERT says, researchers suggest this was partly because of local folklore handed down through generations that helped residents recognise the warning signs
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch1 Oceans and Life (First ed. Sept 2026)
note: Single source, NCERT's own 'researchers suggest'. The research paper / UNESCO source was not read. Use as a 'guess first' story only with the hedge 'NCERT says researchers suggest'. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Wording tightened: NCERT iest201 p.9 says 'largely spared' and 'partly'; 'most people survived because' overstated it.

claim: India's Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) at INCOIS, Hyderabad, under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, was set up after the 2004 tsunami and has been operational since October 2007; it can detect tsunamigenic earthquakes in the Indian Ocean or the global oceans within 10 minutes and sends advisories by email, fax, SMS, GTS and website, 24 hours a day
source: INCOIS (MoES), Information on UNESCO-IOC Tsunami Ready Programme in India
second_source: INCOIS / Indian Tsunami Early Warning System site, About Tsunami Service Providers
note: INC_TSP: ITEWC is the national authority to issue tsunami advisories for India. NCERT Class 7 p.35 (older book) says no early warning exists in the Indian Ocean, and NCERT Class 11 p.59 says India 'volunteered to join' an international system: both are out of date (CORRECTED). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Dates confirmed in INCOIS text: ITEWC operational since October 2007; no day given. NCERT-out-of-date remark stands (Class 7 p.35 says no Indian Ocean warning system; Class 11 p.59 says India 'has volunteered to join'). Status stays CONFIRMED because the row is about ITEWC; the NCERT corrections are in this note.

claim: UNESCO's IOC designated ITEWC a Regional Tsunami Service Provider for the Indian Ocean on 12 October 2011, so it now serves the Indian Ocean rim countries (24 countries in 2017, 25 in the title of a Sept 2020 release)
source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Early Warning for Tsunami and Earthquake (29 Mar 2017)
second_source: INCOIS (MoES), About Us
note: INCOIS About Us confirms the RTSP designation (no date given there). The 2020 PIB (PRID 1657421) was saved but its body was not matched for the date. Claims differing between 'since 2011' and 'since 2012' appear in the two releases; use 2011. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Corrections to the earlier note: PIB 1657421 (21 Sep 2020, Dr Harsh Vardhan) body does say 25 Indian Ocean countries; no saved file says RTSP since 2012, so the 2011-v-2012 remark is unsupported. 12 Oct 2011 and 24 countries (29 Mar 2017) confirmed in PIB 1486040; INCOIS About Us names the RTSP designation without a date.

claim: ITEWC's seismic input in 2017: about 400 seismometers received in real time, automatic detection of earthquakes of magnitude 4.0 and above anywhere on Earth, and a first bulletin with location, magnitude and depth, refined afterwards
source: PIB (Ministry of Earth Sciences), Early Warning for Tsunami and Earthquake (29 Mar 2017)
note: Dated 2017. Current counts not read (G3-A58).

claim: The warning chain in NCERT Grade 9: detection by a network of seismic stations; confirmation by Ocean Bottom Pressure Recorders on the sea floor; tracking by coastal tide gauges and radars; warnings sent by satellite to government agencies and by SMS to officials and the public. ITEWC alerts the Government of India, which informs states and emergency teams
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch1 Oceans and Life (First ed. Sept 2026)
second_source: INCOIS (MoES), Information on UNESCO-IOC Tsunami Ready Programme in India
note: INCOIS pdf lists email, fax, SMS, GTS and website. NCERT also says buoys are part of ITEWC's initiative (p.12). Names the IOC/UNESCO Tsunami Ready scheme in G3-A57.

claim: Design of the system in 2010: 10-12 bottom pressure recorders (able to sense a 1 cm change in water level in up to 6 km of water), about 50 real-time tide gauges and a 17-station broadband seismic network were planned; by then 4 BPRs in the Bay of Bengal and 2 in the Arabian Sea had been deployed of 12 planned (NDMA para 3.1.8; it also says the 17-station seismic network was 'envisaged')
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: Historical (2010). Do not show as current numbers (G3-A58). [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NDMA says BPRs (bottom pressure recorders), not buoys; the 17-station network was 'envisaged to be established by IMD'.

claim: India's warning logic (NDMA): coasts within 60 minutes travel time from a tsunami-making quake get a Warning, Alert or Watch from earthquake data and modelled run-up alone, because there is no time to wait for sea-level data; farther coasts are upgraded to Warning only after water-level confirmation. Warning = expected run-up above 2 m (evacuate); Alert = 0.5 to 2 m (avoid beaches, officials prepare); Watch = under 0.5 m. Bulletins: earthquake information T+20 min, warning/alert/watch T+30 min
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
note: Single source, 2010. Present-day thresholds at INCOIS were not read. Teach as 'NDMA guidelines of 2010 set three levels'.

claim: Tsunami Ready: a UNESCO-IOC community programme with 11 indicators; in 2020 UNESCO-IOC recognised Venkatraipur (Ganjam) and Noliasahi (Jagatsinghpur) in Odisha, making India the first country in the Indian Ocean region and Odisha the first state to get it; a National Board chaired by the Director of INCOIS oversees it
source: INCOIS (MoES), Information on UNESCO-IOC Tsunami Ready Programme in India
note: Single source (INCOIS). Number of Tsunami Ready communities in 2026 not read.

claim: Current number of Bottom Pressure Recorders, tide gauges and seismic stations in India's tsunami system, and the 2026 alert criteria
note: INCOIS pages for the live network were not located. Search snippets named a 2026 Lok Sabha reply on early-warning performance (PIB PRID 2226879) that was not opened.

claim: NDMA's 2010 tsunami guidelines call for bio-shields (mangrove and shelterbelt belts), land-use rules and structural measures along the coast as part of mitigation, besides warning and awareness
source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Tsunamis (Aug 2010)
page_or_section: Contents: Ch.4 Structural Measures, Ch.5 Regulation (5.1 Land Use, 5.2 Bio-Shields); pp.45-65
note: Contents-page level read only; detail pages of ch.4-5 not summarised. Needed for UPSC 2017 GS3 Q18 (preparedness mechanisms in the light of NDMA 2010): Ch.3 Preparedness, Ch.4 Structural, Ch.5 Techno-legal, Ch.6 Emergency Response.

claim: Bhuj earthquake, 26 January 2001: NCERT Class 7 says magnitude 6.9 on the Richter scale; the USGS catalog says M 7.7 (moment magnitude, depth 16 km, about 23.4 N 70.2 E, near 03:16:40 UTC = about 08:46 IST); GSDMA's memorial page says 7.9 on the Richter scale
source: USGS ComCat earthquake catalog, FDSN event web service (official API)
second_source: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Smritivan earthquake memorial page
note: NCERT p.14; GSDMA Smritivan page. IST time is our conversion. Three numbers in three official-looking sources; use USGS 7.7 and say others differ. Epicentre was near Bhachau, Kutch (USGS 'place'), Bhuj being the nearest big town.

claim: Bhuj toll: GSDMA's page says the earthquake affected 15,23,562 people 'from the Kutch district alone', 'killing around 12,932 people and affecting 890 villages' (the sentence does not clearly say the 12,932 deaths are Kutch-only); its memorial carries almost 13,000 victims' names. NDMA says more than 7,900 villages in 21 districts of Gujarat suffered damage. NCERT's school figures: at least 971 students and 31 teachers feared dead
source: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Smritivan earthquake memorial page
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: NDMA07 p.7 (para 1.2.2). A Gujarat-wide official death figure was NOT found at an allowed source (see Part E). NCERT Class 7 p.14 headline box. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] GSDMA's sentence attaches 'Kutch district alone' to the affected count; whether 12,932 is Kutch-only or the toll is unclear. The page is a memorial description, not a statistical release. NDMA's 7,900 villages in 21 districts (p.7 para 1.2.2) and NCERT 971 students/31 teachers confirmed.

claim: After the 2001 earthquake the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) was set up and registered as a society on 8 February 2001, the first state disaster body of its kind created in response; its Smritivan memorial uses 50 check-dam reservoirs to hold victims' nameplates
source: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Smritivan earthquake memorial page
note: Single source. 'First of its kind' is NOT claimed; only the date. Fun story: a memorial that recharges groundwater.

claim: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Act 53 of 2005, passed 23 December 2005) defines a disaster as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence from natural or man-made causes, accident or negligence, causing substantial loss of life or suffering or damage to property or environment, and beyond the coping capacity of the affected community. NCERT Class 11 reproduces this definition but calls it the 'Disaster Management Bill, 2005'
source: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Act 53 of 2005), copy on ndmindia.mha.gov.in (original text; India Code copy returned HTTP 504)
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: NCERT p.68 and the Conclusion call it a Bill and say the Bill was 'introduced': it became an Act in 2005. Section 2(d) text may have a later Explanation (G3-A65); the original text is what was read. India Code copy returned HTTP 504 on 11 Nov 2026. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NCERT p.68 reproduces the definition loosely: it omits 'property' ('damage to, and destruction of, environment') and the 'degradation' limb; Act s.2(d) text and 23 Dec 2005 date confirmed in the saved copy.

claim: The Act sets up a three-level system: the National Disaster Management Authority headed by the Prime Minister, State Authorities headed by Chief Ministers and District Authorities; NDMA published its earthquake guidelines in April 2007 and tsunami guidelines in August 2010 under this Act
source: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Act 53 of 2005), copy on ndmindia.mha.gov.in (original text; India Code copy returned HTTP 504)
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: NDMA07 Preface (pdf p.23) describes the multi-tiered system; NDMA10 p.xxii and §1.x states guidelines are issued as stipulated in the DM Act, 2005.

claim: The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 got the President's assent on 29 March 2025 and came into force on 9 April 2025
source: PIB (Ministry of Home Affairs), Disaster Management (Amendment) Bill, 2024 reply (22 Jul 2025)
page_or_section: para 1 of the Ministry of Home Affairs reply
second_source: Gazette of India Extraordinary, Disaster Management (Amendment) Bill 2024 (Bill 98 of 2024, 1 Aug 2024)
note: What the Act changed in section 2(d) and elsewhere was NOT read in its final form (only the 2024 Bill, which would add an Explanation to 2(d) and new definitions of 'disaster risk' and 'hazard'). Do not claim the exact wording; mark UNVERIFIED for content. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] Dates rest on one MHA written Lok Sabha reply (Shri Nityanand Rai, PIB 22 Jul 2025). The 'second source' is the 2024 Bill, which says it comes into force on a date notified, so it does not corroborate assent or commencement.

claim: NCERT Class 11 describes three stages of disaster management: pre-disaster (data, vulnerability maps, awareness, planning), during disaster (evacuation, shelters, relief) and post-disaster (rehabilitation, recovery, capacity-building); it also says about two-thirds of India's area and an equal share of population are vulnerable to disasters
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Stages: single NCERT source (fine as NCERT statement). The 'two-thirds' figure is NCERT-only; not checked at NDMA/MHA this run.

claim: NCERT Class 11 earthquake mitigation steps: monitoring centres (GPS can track plate movement), vulnerability maps, modified house types and discouraging high-rise buildings in vulnerable areas, and mandatory earthquake-resistant designs and light materials
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: NDMA, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes (Apr 2007)
note: NDMA07 p.7-8 stresses that most Indian buildings in suburban and rural areas are non-engineered and that casualties come mainly from building collapse; traditional houses like Kutch bhongas, Kashmir dhajji diwari are cited as earthquake-resistant.

claim: Earthquakes are 'by far the most unpredictable and highly destructive' of natural disasters in NCERT Class 11 India: Physical Environment's words (kegy106 p.54); the Fundamentals text (kegy203 p.21) lists effects: ground shaking, settlement, landslides, liquefaction, fires, structural collapse, floods from dam failure, tsunami; NCERT says the tsunami effect needs an epicentre under the ocean and a large magnitude
source: NCERT Class XI Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Ch3 Interior of the Earth (Rationalised ed. Dec 2022; Reprint 2026-27)
second_source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Table 6.2 in K106 p.57 groups effects on ground, on man-made structures and on water. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] The quoted phrase is in kegy106 p.54 (Earthquakes), not kegy203 p.21; kegy203 p.21 holds the effects list (12 items) and the tsunami condition, which were confirmed.

claim: Oceans: tides are caused by the pull of the Sun and Moon; spring tides at full and new moon, neap tides at quarter moons (so tsunami is not a tide)
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NOAA / US National Tsunami Warning Center, Tsunami Frequently Asked Questions
note: Used only to show why 'tidal wave' is the wrong name. Full tide mechanism belongs to GEO-11.

claim: Ocean waves are made by wind scraping the surface; the stronger the wind, the bigger the wave; waves carry energy, with wavelength the distance between two crests; a tsunami is a different kind of wave (earthquake, volcano or underwater landslide shifts a mass of water)
source: NCERT Class VII Our Environment, Ch5 Water (Reprint 2024-25; older Class 7 book)
second_source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch1 Oceans and Life (First ed. Sept 2026)
note: I201 p.4 Fig 1.3 (wavelength, crest, trough, wave height, period, frequency). NOAA FAQ 3.x adds the wavelength contrast: miles for tsunamis, far shorter for wind waves.

claim: Ocean-floor relief is where tsunami sources sit: ocean trenches are the deepest parts; Mariana Trench (Pacific) is the deepest place on Earth; mid-ocean ridge is the longest mountain range; seamounts are often volcanic
source: NCERT Grade 9 Understanding Society: India and Beyond Part 2, Ch1 Oceans and Life (First ed. Sept 2026)
second_source: USGS This Dynamic Earth, Plate tectonics and people
note: USGS This Dynamic Earth: subduction zones are marked by trenches. Link used in the video: trench = subduction zone = big quakes and tsunamis. NCERT's 'Mid-Ocean Ridge is the longest mountain range' length is covered in GEO-04. [Audit 11 Nov 2026] NCERT iest201 says 'often volcanic', not 'usually'.

claim: Remote sensing can show tsunami damage: Class 11 Practical Work shows before-and-after satellite images of Banda Aceh, Indonesia (June 2004 and after the tsunami)
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
page_or_section: p.59 refers readers to Practical Work in Geography Part I (NCERT, 2025)
note: The reference sentence is read; the images themselves (kegy306 text lines 361-365) are NCERT figures and are not reproduced.

claim: NCERT classifies natural disasters in four groups: atmospheric, terrestrial, aquatic and biological; earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides, avalanches, subsidence and soil erosion are terrestrial, and tidal waves, storm surge, floods and tsunami are aquatic
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
note: Single source (NCERT's own scheme). Note the odd split: a tsunami (made by a terrestrial event) is filed under aquatic. 'Tidal waves' listed separately from 'tsunami' is NCERT's wording.

claim: NCERT separates a natural hazard (a circumstance in nature with the potential to harm people or property) from a disaster (the harm actually done), and says all hazards need not become disasters; coastal cities such as Mumbai and Chennai are made vulnerable to cyclones and tsunamis by building up to the shore
source: NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment, Ch6 Natural Hazards and Disasters (Revised ed.; Reprint 2026-27)
page_or_section: pp.54-55 (Natural Hazards and Disasters : Causes, Consequences and Management)
second_source: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 (Act 53 of 2005), copy on ndmindia.mha.gov.in (original text; India Code copy returned HTTP 504)
note: Act s.2(d) (G3-A63) defines a disaster by harm and by the community's coping capacity: the same idea in legal words. Lines on Mumbai and Chennai are NCERT's view; no data were read.
